title: Angles, Parallel Lines, and Angle Relationships

objective.objectiveLatex: Identify and classify angles formed by parallel lines and a transversal, vertical angles, complementary and supplementary pairs, and apply the triangle angle sum and polygon angle sum theorems to find unknown angle measures.

prerequisites.noteLatex: Familiarity with basic angle notation and triangle interior angles from prior modules is assumed.

concept.conceptLatex:
When two lines intersect, four angles are formed, and they come in two pairs of vertical angles: each angle shares only its vertex with its vertical partner, with no ray lying between them. Vertical angles are congruent, and the two pairs together make a full turn, so the four measures add to $360^{\circ}$. Know one angle at an intersection and every other angle at that intersection follows.

Two adjacent angles that together form a straight line are a linear pair, and a linear pair is supplementary: the two measures add to $180^{\circ}$. Complementary pairs, which add to $90^{\circ}$, appear wherever a right angle is split into two parts.

When two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, eight angles appear and their relationships are fixed. Corresponding angles, in the same relative position at the two intersections, are congruent. Alternate interior angles, inside the parallel lines but on opposite sides of the transversal, are congruent, and so are alternate exterior angles. Consecutive interior angles, inside on the same side of the transversal, are supplementary. Each of these has a converse: a pair of congruent or supplementary angles cut by a transversal forces the lines to be parallel, which is how most converse proofs of parallel lines are built.

The triangle angle sum generalises the linear pair. For any triangle $\triangle ABC$, $\angle A + \angle B + \angle C = 180^{\circ}$, because the exterior angle at one vertex equals the sum of the two remote interior angles. Cutting a convex $n$-gon into $n - 2$ triangles from a single vertex gives an interior angle sum of $(n - 2) \times 180^{\circ}$, and the $n$ exterior angles, one at each vertex, always add up to $360^{\circ}$.

Choosing which rule applies is mostly a matter of what the figure hands you. A single intersection means vertical angles and linear pairs. Two parallel lines and a transversal mean corresponding, alternate, and consecutive pairs. A triangle means the angle sum. An $n$-gon means the polygon formula, and in a regular polygon every interior angle is equal, so one angle and the vertex count determine all the rest.

examples.titleLatex: Worked example: angles at a single intersection
examples.bodyLatex:
Four angles meet at one point, named in order $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$.

A full turn is $360^{\circ}$, so $\alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta = 360$.

Opposite angles are vertical, so $\alpha = \gamma$ and $\beta = \delta$. If $\alpha = 50$, then $\gamma = 50$, and $2 \cdot 50 + 2\beta = 360$, which gives $\beta = \delta = 130$.

The same value falls out of the linear pair alone: $\alpha + \beta$ is a straight line, so $\beta = 180 - 50 = 130$. Vertical angles are what tell you the fourth angle without a second subtraction.

examples.titleLatex: Worked example: a transversal through parallel lines
examples.bodyLatex:
Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal, forming eight angles.

Four of them are acute, and the other four are their supplements. Since the four acute angles are congruent, all four measure the same value, call it $t$, and each obtuse angle measures $180 - t$.

Consecutive interior angles are supplementary, so one acute and one obtuse angle on the same side of the transversal add to $180$, which is exactly $t + (180 - t)$. That identity is what makes $t$ free to be anything.

For a transversal making an acute angle of $35$, the four acute angles are $35^{\circ}$ and the four obtuse angles are $145^{\circ}$.
examples.answerLatex: the four acute angles are $35^{\circ}$ and the four obtuse angles are $145^{\circ}$

examples.titleLatex: Worked example: interior angles of a regular polygon
examples.bodyLatex:
Take a regular pentagon and draw the diagonals from one vertex.

That triangulates the pentagon into $5 - 2 = 3$ triangles. The diagonals lie inside, so they add no angle of the pentagon itself, and the three triangles account for the entire interior angle sum.

Each triangle contributes $180^{\circ}$, so the sum is $3 \cdot 180 = 540^{\circ}$.

Because the pentagon is regular, its five interior angles are equal, so each one is $540 / 5 = 108^{\circ}$.

items.titleLatex: Confusing vertical angles with adjacent angles
items.wrongLatex: \angle A = \angle B \text{ because they look the same size but share a ray}
items.whyLatex: \text{Vertical angles must be opposite each other at an intersection; adjacent angles share a ray and their sum is not guaranteed to be equal.}
items.fixLatex: \text{Look for the shared vertex and no intersecting segments between the angles. If they share a ray, they are adjacent, not vertical.}

items.wrongLatex: \angle 1 and \angle 2 are corresponding because they are both on the same side
items.whyLatex: \text{Corresponding angles must be in the same relative position at each intersection. Being on the same side alone is not sufficient.}
items.fixLatex: \text{Match the position at one intersection to the same position at the other intersection (top-left with top-left, bottom-right with bottom-right, etc.).}

items.titleLatex: Forgetting to use triangle angle sum in the correct orientation
items.wrongLatex: \angle x = 180^{\circ} - (\angle A + \angle B) \text{ when the triangle is not oriented with a base}
items.whyLatex: \text{The triangle angle sum theorem applies to interior angles regardless of orientation, but one must correctly identify which three angles belong to the triangle.}
items.fixLatex: \text{Identify the three interior angles of the triangle explicitly before applying the theorem.}
